utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Mr. Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-02-60-T, The Prosecutor versus Vidoje Blagojevic and Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning. Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Did you have a good rest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Did you watch the soccer game yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did, indeed. A good game.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it's okay. And we'll let you enjoy the soccer game during the weekend. Are you ready to start?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm ready to start, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning Judge Vassylenko. Good morning, Mr. Karremans.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I just want to go back and touch on a few points from yesterday. Before testifying at the 61, the Rule 61 hearing back in 1996, you gave a statement to the Office of the Prosecution in 1995; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember. During the period after I returned to Zagreb until the first time I appeared here, I delivered several testimonies. There were so many that I have forgotten the sequence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But I have a statement here taken 28 September 1995, and you were questioned by a Mr. Mark Harmon, who is currently working and was working back then with the Office of the Prosecution. Does that refresh your memory?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And that gentleman was the same gentleman that in fact questioned you during the Rule 61 hearing; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's also correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, before testifying at that hearing, did you meet with Mr. Harmon so he could prepare you for your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The meeting took place at Assen in September, as far as I remember, in September 1995, and I was here sometime in August 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But I'm speaking about the time that you testified here in The Hague, in other words, before he put you on the stand and asked you questions --

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not that I remember. It was all so swift that the day of delay from New York. I think that no prior meeting took place with Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, before coming here to testify for the Defence, the Defence asked you to come at least one day before so they could go over all of the documents and to go over the testimony; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, it's not that it could be. My colleague here, Mr. Aleksander Mominov, called you on several occasions. In fact, I have a phone bill that looks more like a king's ransom, where he's discussed over and over you coming here in advance so we could go over all of the documents with you so you'd be prepared, and you would know exactly what sort of questions we would be asking you. Isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where you want to go. But if you want to pay a ransom, I don't mind. When I see the pile of documents that were presented here yesterday, then I think I could have come two days in advance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, we tried to ask you to come two days in advance, then we went to one day, and then we asked you to come, in fact, on the first flight. Isn't that a fact, sir?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. For personal reasons, I came later. I could also have been on holidays in Brazil for three months, if you see what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Exactly. Now, when you did come and we did meet for approximately 30 minutes or so, I did ask whether you could at least spare us one hour, did I not, so I could go over in detail what we had planned to show you and question you about. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you said that you were meeting with your lawyers, and therefore you had no time; right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had an appointment at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Exactly. And then I suggested that after your appointment, I would be available throughout the entire night and that you had our phone numbers so you could contact us so we could go over all of these documents for you, so you would be well prepared to take -- to testify; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was given telephone numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But you were also given the option to come and meet with the Defence to go over the documents and in fact show you even the video; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Objection. Relevancy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The relevancy, Your Honour, was yesterday raised by both Prosecutors. They both stood up on different occasions, both saying that I was not -- I was presenting documents not shown to the gentleman. I'm now trying to show that the gentleman was given an opportunity and chose not to avail himself, and therefore I cannot be held responsible for him not knowing what documents I'm showing him. Because there was an allegation, an allegation - I'm going to put it in those strong terms - that somehow I was being unfair, and I want to show that perhaps there were other reasons --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, well, well, Mr. Karnavas. We come back again, you know. Yes. I -- in this objection, I agree with Prosecution, you know. We don't think there's any relevance to this issue. I believe that you're diligent and you did your best to prepare this witness. There's no doubts, at least from the point of the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Please move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. If I may ask just one last question, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: After meeting with your lawyers did you watch the football game? The Dutch were playing that night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Is that relevant?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It is relevant because it goes to his choice, whether football versus preparation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: As for the details of the proofing session, I think it's a matter between you and your witness. I don't think is that relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Please move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again, and I don't want to -- I will be moving on. Yesterday there was some sort of a discussion as to whether this was cross or direct. In my opinion, it was sort of a soft -- an in-between, a hybrid, but there was a reason, and that's why we asked for the Court's indulgence, and we did get some indulgence from the Prosecution, and I want to thank them for that and I expect some of that indulgence to be carried over on to today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, yesterday was yesterday. It has --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I just said, I expect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Don't bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We have Mr. McCloskey standing up. There's no need for Mr. McCloskey to stand up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We do understand the position Mr. Karnavas is in with Colonel Karremans, and we respect that, and we know Colonel Karremans can defend himself and answer questions. So we are certainly doing that. But coming at him like this about soccer matches and bringing out attorneys, this is designed perhaps to inflame the witness. We have a long day with this witness. He will need his patience and his energy to deal with questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But to go over him in a personal way like this, in the morning --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This is for the press. This is for the press.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I hope both parties please sit down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Please sit down. Well, I'm very sorry, you know, that I mentioned the soccer game first because I want to have this witness relaxed, you know. Sometimes, you know, after a long day's sitting, you have to relax. But I don't think it's proper for the parties, in front of the witness, to argue with each other. It is indeed that we have a very long day and the registrar has done his best to arrange all the facilities for us. We have the morning session in the Courtroom I, but in the afternoon we have to move to Courtroom III. But anyway, we have to finish the testimony of this witness today. Mr. Karnavas promised us that today there are a lot of specific and substantial issues he would like to brought up to this witness. So let's concentrate on our business today and try to finish the testimony of this witness as soon as possible. So from now on, I hope both parties should refrain themselves from mentioning the other party and concentrate on the case in front of us. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Please move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Karremans, I want to show you a film from 1995, July 11th, the first film, only a portion of it. We have it all cued up. I think it's very relevant. I think it's about six minutes long. That's the only film that we will be watching, and I have some questions to ask you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: With the Court's indulgence, if I could be seated, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, of course. If you are not going to ask any questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We're going to watch the whole part and we won't have to watch it again and then I'll ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: "Colonel KARREMANS: ... we collected those weapons. General MLADIC: What do you want?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I've been asked for the meeting ... I had a talk with General Nicolai two hours ago, and also with the national authorities about the request on behalf of the population. It's a request because I'm not in a position to demand anything. We -- the Command in Sarajevo has said that the enclave has been lost and that I've been ordered by BH Command to take care of all the refugees and are now approximately 10.000 women and children within the compound of Potocari, and the request of the BH Command is to -- let's say, to negotiate or ask for the withdrawal of the battalion and withdrawal of those refugees, and if there are possibilities to assist that withdrawal. There are some women who are able to speak English. And what I've heard from all the soldiers who are now working to, let's say, to ease the pain for the population. A lot of people, a lot of persons, women, said: "We are waiting for the bus. Then we leave the enclave." Because they are sick, they are tired, they are very scared. And I've been asked by General Nicolai, asked for, let's say, for a kind of humanitarian support, like food and medicines. Because even in my battalion, I don't have fuel, almost nothing, fuel left, because of the rejection of all the clearances of the last four months. We have been situated in a very poor situation the last four months. That's why I was not able to do the military job. That's why I put most of my efforts in assisting, assisting the military -- Colonel KARREMANS: Yeah, I normally do smoke, sir. Normally I do smoke. But I smoked so much the last days [Inaudible].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: That is concerning the observation post, the OP. Colonel KARREMANS: That's a personal remark. That I'd like to thank the Bosnian Serb military for treating my soldiers well. General MLADIC: No need for that, thanks. They are here, in the hotel. If you keep bombing they won't be hosts for a long time. We can bomb also [Inaudible] and how do you see the result, the resolution of the situation here? Colonel KARREMANS: If I may say something about it, it's not the -- maybe not the same as what they will say in Sarajevo. In my opinion, the enclave will be ended, and that for the sake of the population and not for the sake of the BiH, I should assist the population as much as possible, get out of the enclave to I don't know where they like to go. I think that most of them would like to go to Tuzla, I had been there once three months ago. And in my opinion, they have a better way of living than what I've seen in the enclave. They are living in a very miserable - how do you call it? - way, with the very small means I had within the battalion, medicines and food, we have assisted those people as much as I can. That's one of my tasks, also as a human.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: You have assisted them more than you needed to. Colonel KARREMANS: I'm there for assisting the civil population, not the military side.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: You are all here to help the Muslims and the Croats, especially that guy of yours, van den Broek. He is one of those who destroyed our dream and our joint state [Inaudible]."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you for that, and normally I would show the entire film so as to make sure that there's no implication that we're trying to hide anything. I think we've seen the appropriate portion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Karremans, does that refresh your memory of the events back on that day?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, General Mladic asked you at one point: What do you want? You asked for the meeting. Could you please tell us whether you did in fact ask for a meeting, that it was you that initiated this.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prior to the definitive reception of a fax from Sarajevo, from General Nicolai, I talked to him verbally and I was requested to get in touch as soon as possible with Bratunac. That was possible, because the interpreter in Bratunac, Mr. Petar, was in touch with the battalion. I asked him to organise a meeting in order to discuss a number of points which I was requested to discuss, and secondly, to discuss the situation in and around the compound and to ask for humanitarian support, that is, as you have seen in the film, particularly food and medicines.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, just to make sure: It was General -- you had a conversation with General Nicolai prior to this meeting, at which point he --

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And then he was the one that ordered you or suggested to you, but I take it that generals give orders, to meet with the VRS, and as -- now, the answer is no. Was it a yes or a no that you had a conversation with General Nicolai and he ordered you to have a meeting? Because the screen says "no."

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had a meeting prior -- my first meeting in Bratunac, various meetings have taken place, various talks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, I don't want to interrupt you. I'm talking about prior to Bratunac. I'm talking about before going and meeting with General Mladic, did you have any contact with your higher-ups? Is that what you were referring earlier when you mentioned General Nicolai?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And what were the marching orders that General Nicolai gave you? What did he order you to do? Because generals give orders. I'm not interested in your book, sir. What orders did General Nicolai give you? You're under oath. You need to testify.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would be interested in my book because it describes exactly what orders I got and what requests were made. And don't blame me if I don't remember all of that by heart. I would prefer to take the text and read it out to you slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, before we get to the text, I just want to get the general gist of this. It was based on your conversations with General Nicolai that you then organised a meeting in Bratunac; correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not organise a meeting in Bratunac. I put it down through the interpreter, the man is called Petar, to see if we could come to a conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And who did you ask Petar to contact as your counterpart?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In section 5, in the main building, we had the means of communication whereby we could get in touch with this interpreter, and it was section 5 whom we asked to try and get in touch and try to set up a meeting or a conversation. There was another possibility, but I'm not sure if we used that. We had a number of vehicles present in Bratunac which had been seized, to put it mildly, seized the days before that. And in these vehicles, means of communication are present, and we were in touch with a number of people when, when needed, in order to be able to communicate in that way as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Karremans, I think we could get through this rather quickly if you'd just answer my questions. My earlier question was: Who were you asking Petar to contact? Because obviously he was only an interpreter. So who were you asking to meet with? That's all. Simple question.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Section 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Who is section 5?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Section 5 consists of a number of people, and to make -- not -- to avoid making the answer too long, section 5 is sufficient to me. It could have been someone from section 5, either Mr. Boering, who I understand has been here already, or the general major you have also seen on the film.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Obviously there's a miscommunication. You indicated that with Petar, who was the interpreter and had contacts in Bratunac, you were asking him to see if a meeting could be arranged so you could meet with Serb officers. Do I have that right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Petar was the interpreter on the Bosnian Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. With whom did you ask Petar to meet?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just explained. Someone from section 5. That's either Major Boering or the sergeant-major you just saw in the film. You should not ask me now who arranged that. One of the people of section 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Karremans, I'm not asking you who arranged the meeting. You were a lieutenant colonel. You were the commanding officer. You had the responsibility of the people, as well as the life of your own soldiers. So you were the highest-ranking officer. Obviously, you wanted to meet with somebody on the other side if General Nicolai had asked you to negotiate. So my question to you is: With whom were you asking to negotiate? Was it Karadzic? Was it Mladic? Who was it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think a proper question would be just to ask Mr. Karremans --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I object, Your Honour, to the coaching of the witness through this --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No. I'm trying to be --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The gentleman --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, well, well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We have to be easy, easy, easy. We come back again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the gentleman --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, if both parties are not at ease this morning, we'll stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I believe I'm entitled to do my questioning. The gentleman did indicate that he did not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I don't think so, Mr. Karnavas. I think the gentleman, the witness, has already answered your question. You know, I think you have to have a follow-up question. Because, you know, are you expecting to meet Mr. Mladic, you know, in the Fontana Hotel? How did he turn up, you know. Certain things. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll go around it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll go around it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Take it easy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Karremans, did you know General Mladic at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you get a briefing before you left the Netherlands as to who General Mladic was?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you ask to meet with General Mladic on that day?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Who did you ask to meet with?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Standard procedure under these conditions is to contact the commanding officer of the party involved in the conflict, whoever that may be. I don't really care with the commanding officer as I am of DutchBat, they also had a commanding officer, whether it was General Mladic or Ivanovic or whomever. The commanding officer. Why? To do business.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So just to be clear: You asked to meet with the commanding officer; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, you had been in that area for close to six months. Did you know who the commanding officer was that you were expecting to meet?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I expected to meet General Zivanovic, commander of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you specifically ask to meet with General Zivanovic or did you just say the commanding officer? Which of the two?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not ask, but I did expect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, did you know -- did you know General Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not meet him previously. Upon the transfer in January, I received some information about him from my predecessor, but there was never any time or opportunity to meet him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That entire time that you were there when this humanitarian crisis was going on, as you indicated, inside the enclave, you never requested to meet with General Zivanovic, the commanding officer?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Is there a reason why you didn't ask to meet with General Zivanovic either before or at the commencement or during the activities regarding Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No time is not the right answer, but no time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You didn't have the time to place a call to Petar, as you did that afternoon, to meet with the commanding officer, is that what you're suggesting, during that six-month period?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No time and no opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So it wasn't that you were not instructed; you had orders not to make contact with the commanding officer in the area, but it was that you had no time or no opportunity?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, could you please tell us what you had heard about General Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very briefly, that it's the commander is a straightforward person. We would call that Burgundian, boorish type in Holland, a big person that would be good for doing business with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And I take it you -- when you went to Bratunac, you were rather taken aback by the manner -- the person that you did ultimately meet and started doing business with?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: After six days of war and three months of not having left the area, we entered a hotel and expected to speak to the commanding officer. I did not expect somebody I'd never seen before in my life. I expected at least to see General Mladic there. So I was expected.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, when the gentleman began speaking to you, did you ask for him to identify himself or did you recognise immediately that this in fact was General Mladic, the highest commanding officer of the VRS army?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted to set something straight. He didn't start talking. He started screaming. And second, I didn't realise it was General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And it's your testimony that he started screaming before any small talk? We see that on the video.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. And at some point, did you realise that this was General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: At what point?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right from the start.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, at some point in the video, you do say that you talk with -- you had a talk with General Nicolai, and I believe you said, and it's on the video, some time earlier. Could you please tell us: How much time had elapsed from the time you had spoken with General Nicolai and the time that you met General Mladic at the Hotel Fontana?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not very late. I'd have to check my book about the times. I had a conversation with the Dutch authorities that same day, with another section, before I went to this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you say you need to check your book. Are the times and the periods in that book based on a personal diary that you kept in the field, sir?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. This one. Okay. By the way, did you ever make that available to the Office of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did they ever ask you? I mean, this would be pro forma for somebody doing an investigation to ask those questions. Were they ever asked -- did they ever you whether you kept a personal diary?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Oh, okay. And what, pray tell, was the answer you gave them?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: A diary is personal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So, in other words, you told them that you had a diary, but you were not going to make it available to them?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Diary" is not the word I used. I might be mistaken about the words. But it's a book of notes about all my discussions and meetings and what I saw and what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I take it -- go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I tell you about the conversation with General Nicolai? It was at 1755 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 1755. Thank you. Now, I take it you will be making that diary available to us in the event the Trial Chamber were to order you to do so.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And may I ask why not?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I just said, this is a personal item.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, what if you were to take out the personal items, notes to yourself that are personal in nature versus notes that are relevant as to what happened minute by minute during those critical days?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: My personal opinion is that the notes in these notebooks - and there are six of them - that they're personal and that I have -- that I'm not required to disclose them. Aside from whether they're personal notes or times there were matters about staff, their remarks that are nobody else's business. If I remove all of those, then I might as well throw out what's left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I add something?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Go ahead. Add. Because I --

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] One sentence. [Interpretation] I used these notebooks, plus a few other documents, to write my book.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. That's good to know. Did you by any chance make copies of your diaries and provide them to the parliament or to the NIOD?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Were they asked?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. To nobody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did they ask you?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Several cases, I was asked whether they could see them or might copy certain parts or copy everything, and to this day I have always said no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And I take it -- what about the Ministry of Defence? Did they by any chance ask you to provide -- for you to provide them with copies of your notes?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Ministry of Defence is -- has no bearing on this. It was a UN operation and not an operation under one country, such as the Netherlands. I understand where you're headed. The Ministry of Defence conducted investigations as well, but each time I mentioned that I have six of these notebooks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But since this is a UN Tribunal and you were on a UN mission, then it would appear that those notes would be relevant, not -- well, one, relevant, and two, discloseable, since, as you indicated, this was a UN mission. So if the UN Tribunal were to ask you for your notes that you took based on this UN mission, would you provide them, provide us with those notes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think these are now irrelevant issues about whether UN Tribunal and mission. I don't think that's relevant to this issue, although I think the issue itself is relevant, but not this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, let me ask some questions to this witness. Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I understand that you told us that the book you wrote was based somehow on the diaries and the other materials.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And to what extent? I mean, how detailed this book? It's about what happened during that critical period. I mean, for instance, did you mention the time, like 1755, you know, that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you've ever seen my book, there are several annexes at the back which are consistently numbered, TK, those are my initials, and then a number. Most of these annexes include times and time frames. But in the course of the book, there are also some times that are relevant as for when certain services were requested and when they -- when air support was requested and when that was delivered. The second part of the answer is that you can't focus too much on times in a book because it will make the book less readable. But everything in -- everything that's relevant in these notebooks can also be found in my book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I thank you. And are there any English translation for your book?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karnavas, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's move on. I'll try to figure out what to do about these notes at some point. But just to let you know, I will be making a formal request, Mr. Karremans, so you can think about what you want to -- how you want to respond on that. Now, getting back to what we saw on the video: You say on the video that: "I had a talk with General Nicolai two hours and also with the national authorities about the request on behalf of the population." Now, if, according to your notes that you have there, you spoke with General Nicolai on 1755, then now we're talking about, what, 1955? So that would be around, what, 8.00, 8.00 p.m., that you actually meet with -- when you met with General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, turn that --

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's also in my notebook what time it was. Because it concerns displacement to Bratunac and passing OP Papa, which was one of our observation posts, and passing what we called OP Jovo, that was mentioned yesterday, and various security measures that were required en route. So I'm not sure exactly what the time of arrival was, but it's indicated in my book what time we arrived and what time we started the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, if you want to look at your book.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yes. [Interpretation] Around 9.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Around 9.00.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] 9.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 9.00. So if you spoke with General Nicolai around 1755, that would be, what, 6.00. We're talking about three hours in between; right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, obviously it would have taken you some time to go from where you were located, go through the checkpoints and go to Bratunac. But could you please tell us: During that period of two hours plus, after speaking with General Nicolai, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think any normal person would do: Eat. Perhaps I did something else. I spoke with the Dutch authorities, if I remember, by telephone. I believe that I spoke by phone to the sector north-east, Colonel Brantz, and another very normal thing is to have a staff meeting, which usually took place at fixed times to hear from the staff officers everything that had been going on. There may have been conversations with the commander of the CARE company about the care of my own men and about humanitarian aid. I may have checked the bandaging unit to visit the wounded. Basically there's too much to mention in detail during a short period. There may be ten other things that happened during that relatively brief period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And is there anything in your notes that you brought with us that is noteworthy, other than what you've mentioned, if you want to refer to it?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: May I ask, are there any entries between General Nicolai and meeting at Hotel Fontana that's based upon?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In my book, you'll find a brief description of what I just talked about. There are only highlights. Please understand that people -- readers get bored if you write that you used the rest room in between. So my book provides highlights to give a good summary of several events.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. I wasn't asking about your book. I was asking about that little notebook. Since we're not going to see it, maybe you can share the relevant information?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to go -- we will touch upon all of these folks that you -- all of these different meetings that you think you might have had. But when you make reference here on the tape with the national authorities, could you please tell us, who are the national authorities? Which authorities are you referring to that we saw in the video?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I say "the national authorities," I mean the KL Crisis Staff representative. KL stands for Royal Air Force, another person would be somebody representing foreign affairs, or somebody representing the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So that would be the Dutch government?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you have any contacts with the national authorities either -- or at the local -- yes, the national authorities of the BiH, in other words, contact somebody in Sarajevo, Izetbegovic, Silajdzic?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not personally. But one of the interpreters in the battalion tried on various occasions to contact Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: To contact -- who exactly were they at that trying to contact, was he trying to contact?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who. He tried to contact Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Was that at his -- at his own initiative or was that on an order given to you -- given by you?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: His own initiative, perhaps requested by Major Franken, but I doubt that, because I was responsible for external communication. And he probably did so at his own initiative.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So I just want to make sure. There's an interpreter working for DutchBat and on his own initiative he's trying to contact the BiH authorities? Would that not be something that you, as the commander, would be responsible for doing?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under those circumstances, things are possible that are not standard procedure or usual. Connections were poor. At first he didn't even get through. And my connections with sector north-east and Sarajevo were not always good either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite possibly, but that's something that I forget about, it's possible that Sarajevo -- rather, BH command General Nicolai asked me to get in touch with Bosnian authorities in Sarajevo. But going back nine years in my memory, it does not seem to be right, because it was easier for the headquarters in Sarajevo to contact the government in Sarajevo than to have this done through the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. In your notes that you have with us, do you have any notations whether General Nicolai had indicated with whom he had communicated prior to his communication with you?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did he say whether he had been given any orders or instructions?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I just want to be crystal clear on this: What exactly did General Nicolai tell you to do, or ordered you to do?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already answered that. You'll find that in one of the annexes to my book, and those annexes are based on my notes in this booklet. So it's crystal clear what was asked at the time and what was confirmed later on with the facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So does that mean that you're not going to tell us you're under oath? Because your book is not under oath; you are.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. [Interpretation] Annex 35 in my book covers the report of the meeting on 11 -- the meetings on 11 and 12 July.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I'm asking about General Nicolai.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I stated earlier, General Nicolai called me at five to 6.00 and gave me several oral assignments -- [In English] [Previous translation continues]... report. [Interpretation] Told me that withdrawing the battalion was in study, under consideration. He asked me to arrange a cease-fire as quickly as possible, which is a cease-fire. And in my response was to briefly describe the situation to him at that time where we were, because he asked me for that. Item 2 in Annex 35 -- [In English] HQ UNPROFOR Sarajevo to enter into local negotiations with BSA forces for immediate cease-fire. [Interpretation] Those would be local negotiations. [In English] I had two meetings with General Mladic. And appendix is [Interpretation] this is Appendix 34.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, in the -- going back to the video, you told General Mladic that you had consulted with the Dutch authorities, or you said national authorities. Now we know it's the -- this crisis group or staff of the Dutch authorities. What instructions had they given you?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: None. They were not capable of giving instructions. That is done via the hierarchical lines, that is, Zagreb-Sarajevo-Tuzla-Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: With whom did you speak?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked that question before. I don't remember who I talked to. There have been so many conversations. I don't remember who I talked to after Crisis Staff or somebody from foreign affairs or someone from the Ministry of Defence. I only know that a conversation took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And there's nothing in your notes that would say a name or an initial?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Who initiated this conversation? Was it you calling them, asking for someone; or they calling you?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: They called me. And in some cases, the conversations took place via sector north-east commander Brantz, who said I have talked to -- this is an example, "I talked to the Minister of Defence and he should like to talk to you at 1800 hours," and then a communication was made and then I talked to the Minister of Defence. Or, "I have talked to the commander of the army and he wants to talk to you at 1700 hours." And then communication was made at 1700 hours and then the conversation took place. That is how the conversations took place at the national level.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karremans. And could you please tell us: Since they initiated a conversation, obviously they must have wanted to convey some kind of a message to you. Perhaps they just wanted to check in on you. But do you recall what was discussed?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not really. But I know that nearly all conversations that took place during that period with the Netherlands - and I'm referring to the Minister of Defence and the commander-in-chief and the commander of the Crisis Staff and so on and so on - that it was always about what is the situation like with the battalion, what is the situation with the refugees, and what do you need, and make sure that the battalion, as DutchBat 3, with the means available, that you provide assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you then said that you think that you had a discussion with the north-east sector. That would be in Tuzla. Do you recall the nature of the conversation and what, if any, orders were given to you then?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The nature of the conversation was the same. As I mentioned earlier, it was a brief sketch of the situation, of what the situation was, and I told him that I had received oral orders, later confirmed by fax, from General Nicolai, how he interpreted this or would interpret this. I asked Colonel Brantz, my contact in the sector north-east, to arrange talks at the much higher level than the level between commander of DutchBat and the commanding officer of, say, the Bosnian Serb forces. The same requests I also made directly to General Nicolai, and apart from that, you know how it goes: They ask you how you're doing yourself, is everything in order, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And I don't want to go into great details, but suffice it to say those requests that you made to have negotiators brought in at a higher level from the UN or elsewhere never materialised, and so you had to -- you were on your own, basically; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you know why the UN wasn't interested in sending a more senior negotiator at the time to assist you, in light of the situation?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I seem to remember that an attempt was made to get two colonels on the way, with or without a mandate from Janvier in order to start negotiations. These colonels never arrived. I raised the issue with General Nicolai several times, saying that someone at the higher level should start negotiations or continue the negotiations. And General Nicolai himself, as Chief of Staff too, was not given approval. In short, nobody came.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And just for the record, Janvier is above General Nicolai, is that correct, in the hierarchy, as things go?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Dat Kloopt."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you later on in that conversation, you say that -- you're there to negotiate or ask for the withdrawal of the battalion and withdrawal of those refugees, if there are possibilities to assist that withdrawal. Now, from that, one would think that perhaps the issue of the withdrawal of the refugees might have been discussed between you and General Nicolai. Could you please tell us whether that topic ever came up.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The issue was discussed, and if we're talking about assisting in the withdrawal, then what is meant by this is to try to keep things in our own hands. And you should try to achieve a certain sequence in which the withdrawal is to take place, namely, first the injured, then the weak, and so on. And there is a second way of interpreting this, namely, that withdrawal should not be discussed at all, but you should stay where you are. And there is a third possibility: Leave it to the people. But that was impossible because I had to face 20.000 to 25.000 refugees in and around the compound. So, in brief, consideration the humanitarian situation, something had to be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And but now if I could go back to the transcript of the video, as we saw the video, we see it starts with General Mladic asking you -- the clip, of course, that I showed you: "What do you want? You asked for the meeting." You talk about that you had talked to General Nicolai. But then it would appear that you're suggesting to him or informing him that you want to negotiate for the withdrawal of those refugees. So Mladic being the listener and not privy to your conversations with General Nicolai, would he not get the impression that you were there seeking to withdraw all of the refugees that were in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That is a matter of interpretation and playing with words. It was the first brief meeting, at which my -- I made the suggestion to talk at least about what should be done with these 20.000 to 25.000 refugees which I had on and around the compound, considering the humanitarian situation. Should we leave them there? Should we let them starve? Because I had no more food. Or should we send them back to the town of Srebrenica, to the shelter project, which was impossible? Or should they be moved somewhere, as they wanted themselves? In brief, it was a consideration of possibilities, and in my opinion, this should come out during a conversation. That is also why I wanted to have talks at a much higher level.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But I'm speaking specifically of your conversations with General Mladic. And the video, unless it's a montage, an issue that is not an issue in this case -- did you see any of that, where you're suggesting possibilities? That's not on the video, is it, Mr. Karremans?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But your thoughts are not on the video, and the circumstances in which this initial meeting took place, and the way I think about it is also not on the video. All sorts of things are on your mind, especially when you face General Mladic for the first time, and you try, in the best possible way, to represent that which has come up at an earlier meeting in order to see whether there is an opening, in any way whatsoever, to be able to come to business.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But you don't dispute the fact that on the video it says that you're there to negotiate for the withdrawal of those refugees. That's -- those are your words; right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was said was said. That is no better evidence than this video film. I just explained to you: The intention of this question was: What shall we do? Shall I get support or do I not get support, and who will give me support? Are we staying where we are, and will we let them starve, or do we send them back, or do we send them elsewhere? That is a normal question under these circumstances. I say explicitly "under these circumstances" because we could also have sat down at a table and conducted normal negotiations and reached an agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, perhaps this may be a good time to take a break, and when we come back, we'll go over part of the video transcript where General Mladic asks you what shall we do? What is your proposal for the resolution of this situation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Let's leave this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's what I said. I just want the gentleman to know where we were going to pick up so he could be aware that's where going.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll resume at a quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Before we begin, Mr. Karremans, let me first apologise if I've given the impression that I'm antagonistic or that you are on trial, because you're not. And so if during the proceedings yesterday or today it seemed that I was overly anxious in getting some of the answers and gave you the wrong impression, I truly apologise, and I hope you accept my apology. So, getting back to where we were -- and incidentally, no one is suggesting that you acted in any way that was improper or should be viewed improperly. Now, getting back to the video, you also indicate that there are some women who speak English and that you've heard from your soldiers that, and I quote. What you say is women are saying: "We are waiting for the buses and can we leave the enclave?" And I've asked -- "I've been asked by General Nicolai, ask for, let's say, for a kind of humanitarian support, like food and medicines." Now, it would appear, would it not, Mr. Karremans, that you had a briefing from your own soldiers that the women, or at least some of the population of the refugees, also wanted to leave the enclave; correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not briefed, but in my answer to one of your earlier questions about what I did with the message I got from General Nicolai around 6.00 and my departure to Bratunac, in the staff meeting, or during talks with people from the battalion, I heard, or I learned, that within the group of refugees, remarks were made to the effect like: Where are the buses, and when can we leave?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And I take it -- [Microphone not activated] -- that the refugees themselves wanted to leave and you were conveying that information to General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yes. Not for all of them, of course. [Interpretation] Not for everyone. Among the refugees, there were people who had always lived in the area. But for the majority of the refugees who had had to leave their homes before, there was only one wish, as far as I understood, from the comments, namely, that they simply wanted to leave the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And then on the video we see General Mladic ask you, and incidentally, for the record, I'm reading from Exhibit P21A, which is the official translation of that video. And this would be from ERN number L0092417. General Mladic asked you: "What is your proposal for the resolution of this situation?" The interpreter interpreted: "How do you see the result, the resolution of the situation here?" And then you say at some point: "Maybe not the same as what they will say in Sarajevo." And then you say: "Because they are the policy makers." And then you go on to say: "In my opinion, the enclave will be ended, and for the sake of the population, and not for the sake of the BiH, I should assist the population as much as possible, get out of the enclave to I don't know where they like to go. I think that most of them would like to go to Tuzla," and so on. And then you also state your opinion: "In my opinion, they have a better way of living than I've seen in the enclave." So it would appear, Mr. Karremans, that you're informing General Mladic that you wanted to assist the population as much as possible, get out of the enclave; correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said and what you have seen in the video is a representation of what I have seen during the months before and what I picked up from the talks. And on the basis of what was discussed with General Nicolai with regard to providing as much humanitarian support as possible. That is also part of, as I said before, of deciding what to do with the 20.000 to 25.000 refugees, leaving them where they were or taking them back to where they came from, or taking them -- letting them go somewhere else. And one of the ways to resolve that is, in normal consultation, to see what is possible. If the possibility had occurred -- and these are the kind of thoughts that emerge in such a situation. If the possibility had occurred of letting people return, and if they could -- if we could have gone back to the situation as it was before July the 6th, so with an enclave border but with normal humanitarian support, then I think that would also have been a good solution. My stake for this conversation was: How can we reach a good solution? And one of the possibilities was to move the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, just to pick up on your answer: As far as having a normal situation in the enclave that would have required a complete demilitarisation of the enclave; correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, would you agree with me that the VRS had some concerns, or the Serb population had some concerns as long as there was the presence of a Muslim army inside the enclave, going out on occasions on various military objectives? Correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] That is correct. [Interpretation] That is correct. It is an option.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. And of course, as the Canadians, as DutchBat 1, DutchBat 2, DutchBat 3, was no more successful in demilitarising the enclave; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think we have spent a lot of time yesterday on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll rephrase. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That possibility, incidentally - that is, the possibility of people returning to the enclave in a demilitarised enclave, with the Dutch remaining there pursuant to their mission - was never discussed on the video, at that meeting, or at any other meeting, or am I wrong?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it was ever discussed, although I do remember what I just said, namely, that it could have been an option. I don't remember if I discussed it at one of the following meetings or whether I ever tabled that. But you'll understand that, under the circumstances that we all know, you need to suggest all the possibilities and take all opportunities in order to improve things for the population, and that was my ultimate assignment, namely, to arrange things as well as possible for the local population.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand --

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: And non-relocation, that is, going back to the situation of departure which existed before July the 6th was of course also an option.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Would you please tell us whether you saw that option on the video being discussed or even proposed or suggested or inferred or insinuated when General Mladic asked you concretely: "What is your proposal for the resolution of this situation?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: That was the same question Mr. Karnavas asked before, and the witness answered: "I don't think that it was ever discussed." And then he added another thought to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Was it ever discussed at any other meetings, so at least the option that you perhaps had in your mind would have been conveyed to your counterparts, the ones that you were negotiating with?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. -- well, Mr. Karnavas, I think the witness also answered that. "I don't remember if I discussed it at one of the following meetings or whether I ever tabled that."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I were to tell you, Mr. Karremans, that on the subsequent videos that we have for the second and the third meeting, and as you saw from the first meeting, there's absolutely no reference to that particular option, would that assist you in refreshing your memory?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you can. If it is not on the video, and it hasn't been taped, then of course that is so. I am not inventing this option here on the spot. It was discussed. Possibly it was in an entirely different setting, under different circumstances, with Major Franken or with section 5, or even with Colonel Brantz, from sector north-east. And perhaps then we came to the conclusion on the basis of a number of arguments that that couldn't be an option. Or, considering the short amount of time that followed this, during the conversation or the next day, which passed immediately into the departure of the refugees, that it was no longer raised and that the only remaining idea was to relocate the people. I hope this answer indicates how short a time period we had to discuss a great many issues, which were not discussed with one single person but which I had to discuss with many people to have good feedback. And at least, let me say, to get indications, instructions, about how to act.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, I'm not disputing, nor am I challenging, the fact that this option might have been, or perhaps was in fact discussed among your men, and perhaps with the higher-ups. The question was whether this option was ever conveyed to the other side. And from your answer, it would appear that a decision -- or it became obvious that option perhaps wasn't available or possible, so it was never conveyed to General Mladic. That's what I'm trying to get at.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So the only option that was discussed was General Mladic's, what we see on the video, that is, you assisting the evacuation of the refugees from Potocari?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I wanted, in the first instance, humanitarian aid, that is, food, medicines, and the evacuations of the injured to hospitals, under the leadership of the International Red Cross or NOMAD, the medical assistance unit of the Norwegians. If I could get food and other things necessary for life in the immediate future, then it would have been able for us to live for a longer period with the refugees in and around the compound. Considering the short amount of time available, all of this was impossible, and that caused the option to arise of relocating the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Karremans, I just want to -- we can get shorter answers out of you. When you met with General Mladic, the only option that you discussed was the assistance of evacuating the entire population that had gathered in Potocari. Isn't that what we saw on the film? I understand how you wanted the evacuation to proceed, that is, the injured, the sick, the elderly, the young, and that eventually the other people, but what we're talking about is the evacuation of the entire population, along with your men. That's what we see on the film and that was the only thing that you had discussed with General Mladic; correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not together with my men. If you want short answers, then I can give you short answers, but I'm afraid that I do not do justice to the situation that occurred. And if the circumstances that the population was in and the battalion was in do not get explained properly, then things like that which was said on the video film may be misinterpreted, despite the fact that it was said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I think we'll move on. Since this period of time, have you had a chance to read the NIOD report?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said in my introduction, I took part in many official and unofficial investigations. Some of them I read. The NIOD report is not in my possession and I did not read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. It's on the Internet, by the way, in case you want to check it out. Now, you said that you did write your book, but that book was written after some period of time; correct? After the events.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I wrote my book during my stay in the United States.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And would it be -- and you indicated that that -- a lot of the facts in the book are based on the notes that you have; right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] That's correct [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But the notes were taken contemporaneous to the events, whereas the book was written after the events and perhaps after everything was being filtered through the, let's say, publicity and the media surrounding the events and thereafter?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. My book was not filtered.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I didn't say your book was filtered, but I'm saying that the notes were written contemporaneous, as things were going on, whereas the book was written upon reflection and at a time and period when, this, the issue of Srebrenica and the behaviour of the DutchBat had come into question. I mean, and that's public knowledge; right? I'm just trying to draw the distinction, one versus the other. One contemporaneous; the other one upon reflection.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: So you're suggesting that there is a difference between what I wrote in my book and what is written in my notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting anything. I'm just merely making a statement, asking you whether you agree with me or not.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Nee."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, I just want to go through some documents here. I have them all laid out. Perhaps we won't need to go through all of them. But I just wanted to ask you: Were you aware of some of the discussions that were ongoing with respect to evacuations and the abandonment of the enclave prior to the events in Srebrenica? Is that a yes?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In fact, there was a particular plan in place for the eventuality, in case the enclave had to be evacuated or DutchBat had to be evacuated, what should be done; correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are operation plans containing options for moving a unit, in this case, DutchBat 3, out of the area, in this case, the CVR.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Had you heard of what was known as Operation Determined Effort, or also, I guess in military parlance, O-plan 40104?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think for me, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, it appears that the DutchBat, in fact, had been asked to fill out a questionnaire as to the feasibility of the evacuation process, and I think they were discussing an evacuation by helicopters. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that sideways, from talks with sector north-east, Colonel Brantz, that this is one of the possibilities, to move the DutchBat unit out of the location. There are more possibilities, of course, but helicopters are one possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. But during those discussions, the possibility was also talked about what to do with the people and the enclave, and the need perhaps to evacuate them as well. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Helicopters are used in principle for military operations or for Medevac, and Medevac are military evacuations. So in other words, military staff or refugees who are injured and had to be taken to a medical installation [as interpreted] as soon as possible. But not to move entire population groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I understand that, Mr. Karremans. What I am asking you is: Was there not a discussion about the evacuation of the people, in general?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're not being clear. We are now talking about -- are we talking about the possible relocation of the battalion or of the population with relation to the helicopters?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Karremans, I'm trying to get you home. Going back to the plan: Plans were discussed at very high levels, and we're going to go through them as a result of the obstacles we're having here. Plans were put in place for potential evacuation, not just of the battalion but of the people as well. Isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That may be right, but I don't know. I only know the plans possibly to move the battalion by helicopter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know whether -- were you privy to any discussions about what to do with the people living in the enclave?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There have been few talks about the options I just indicated to you, because at the higher levels, too, it was understood, or should have been understood, what enormous problems this would involve. In brief, moving the population by helicopter, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm not asking by helicopter. I'm asking -- you indicated the battalion by helicopter. I'm now asking about the population itself, since by helicopter was not an option, as you've indicated. Were other options discussed with respect to the evacuation of the population, or was it your opinion that the DutchBat were just going to cut and run and leave the population there, get in the helicopters and fly away?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me put one thing very clearly here, and on other occasions I've also said this. It has been my conviction - and I repeated this several times - DutchBat will leave no sooner than when all measures have been taken on behalf of the population. Any measures whatsoever. It was offered to us to move out together with the population. In another conversation it was suggested, "You can also leave now with your battalion," and my answer has always been no. First the injured, first the population, and the battalion, we'll see when they leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. And that's exactly my point. Now, were you aware that as early as May, or as early as 1994, at the UN discussions were being held with respect to the evacuation of the enclave and the withdrawal of UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. We don't have to discuss the 1994. By the way, for the record, I'm reading -- I'm making references to the NIOD report. This would be found on part 3, chapter 1, section 8, where it discusses Boutros Boutros-Ghali, discussions of this with Janvier. All right. Now, do you know, of the ongoing discussions as late as the spring of 1995, between May 16 and May 24, regarding the evacuation process, or --

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Would it surprise you to learn that Janvier was pushing for the withdrawal from the -- or the partial withdrawal from the eastern enclaves? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Were you aware that on May 24th, I believe, there was a security consulate that was a closed session, where Janvier, he didn't say explicitly that Srebrenica had to be abandoned, but he did say that UNPROFOR could no longer execute their mission in Eastern Bosnia, which was generally explained as a plea for withdrawal. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps. I know this is a vague answer, but in the talks on the telephone with General Nicolai or with Commander Brantz, we discussed from time to time what went on in the higher levels in Zagreb, and we discussed Janvier from time to time. But the information was minimal. It had little influence on DutchBat's operation at that time, perhaps on a longer time but not then. In other words, the amount of information that came down from the top with regard to these issues which you mentioned was minimal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: And therefore I said no a number of times.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And I'm not suggesting, by the way, that you had this information, but now it's out in the open that apparently these sorts of things were ongoing. Now, in the NIOD report, sticking with this, this is the spring of 1995, and I'm reading from part 3, chapter 1, section 11, it says: "UNPROFOR had lost the consent of the Bosnian Serbs for their presence and were no longer seen as peacekeeper. Certainly hardly be called impartial any more." I'm sorry: "Certainly not since UNPROFOR was withholding four VRS soldiers prisoner of war. UNPROFOR could hardly be called impartial any more and they were not far from that point, that in fact they were allies of the Bosnian Muslims." Is that a correct statement?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know this statement, because if I had made it, perhaps, but I don't think it is my statement. I don't know where it comes from.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in the NIOD report again, and it's talking -- these are discussions that were going on with respect to the potential evacuation of the enclave prior to the events. And again, this could be found on part 3, chapter 1, section 11, on page 6, it says: "Now the Netherlands hope that the following would happen with UNPROFOR. A redeployment of the troops, which would make UNPROFOR less vulnerable, no longer sending armed observers and a new policy regarding the enclaves.
