But if the UN troops left the enclaves, they would have to take along the local population. As said before, Voorhoeve had already expressed the idea in a conversation with Perry." That would be the Secretary of Defence of the United States. "Implementation of this idea would of course mean a lot of human suffering. However, it was better than ethnic cleansing by Bosnian Serbs. Though it meant cooperating with ethnic cleansing, it could be defended in the interest of the population -- of the population were concerned." My question to you, sir, is: Were you aware of these discussions within the Netherlands government?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. It's just easier for the witness -- or almost impossible for the witness to make a comment if he doesn't know what the source of this is. Just from listening to it now, have been given the quote but for the witness it's almost impossible to make a comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. We could put it on the ELMO, but this is again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think this report is in English or in Dutch?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's in English. It's in English, Your Honour. And it's in Dutch as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Do you have the Dutch version?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No. But the gentleman is fluent in English, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour -- I don't mean to quarrel with the Court, but he did spend three years in the United States at a very high level, and I think -- perhaps his speaking is not as fluent, but he's told me -- we had this discussion, how fluent his English was. So I'm not speaking off -- I'm not making this up. But we could ask the gentleman if he feels comfortable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I mean, we would have the Dutch version. It's three volumes. I have it in my office. We can -- if that assists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Let's try that English version first. If impossible, I think we could use that Dutch version.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] Can I respond to that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you. My English is as my Dutch. Because I work for 12 years in NATO assignments and I read as quick the English language as my own language. I prefer to speak in my own language here today and yesterday. [Interpretation] I'm going to switch to Dutch. I heard a text with which I was not familiar and can therefore not respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking you whether you were aware of this.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. That's a response, then. Thank you. I'll take that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Usher. I apologise for the inconvenience. Though I may have some more documents at some point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, before we talk about -- let's go on to see what the NIOD report has to say about your involvement, and I guess the negotiations that were going -- ongoing. And perhaps we can put on the ELMO part 3, chapter 7, section 4. And we're going to stay in the first page a little bit and then we'll move on. There are only a couple of sections. In the first paragraph, we can see that -- I don't want to read the entire paragraph. But in the first paragraph, we note in the middle of it, it says: "In case DutchBat would have to leave the enclave, somehow four options open to DutchBat were discussed: Activation of the NATO withdrawal plan, O plan 40104." That was the plan we discussed earlier. "... a UN and NATO helicopter operation, an escape attempt via the northern edge of the enclave and leaving by road, taking the vehicles. The latter would, however, have to be referred to the Bosnian Serbs and the population would have to be taken along. It was generally feared that the Bosnian Muslims would want to block DutchBat, leaving by lying down in front of the vehicles. The question was also raised as to who would be in charge if one of the options were chosen. The answer was that this would be the UN in the case of the last option driving off, and in the case of the first three options, it would be the United States or NATO." And if we go further up this particular paragraph, it appears that this is a meeting that is taking place at the Defence Crisis Management Centre, which would have been the same crisis management centre that you had spoken with on July 11th; correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. I'm not familiar with this text. I'm not member of the Ministerial Council. Rather, I'm part of the Defence Crisis Management Centre. The three parts of the armed forces - air force, marine, and army - each had their own crisis centre, which maintained contact with the Defence Crisis Management Centre 24 hours a day, is intended to inform the ministers and the Ministerial Council directly with information in these types of situations. Clearly, however, Srebrenica was a secluded part of the world, and we weren't able to keep up with these affairs and certainly in no position to influence them. You mentioned four possibilities for leaving the area; that's true. It's known DutchBat 1, DutchBat 2, and DutchBat 3. There were four opportunities -- opportunities to leave the area with the unit under certain conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So you were aware of these four different options?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And were you aware of these four different options before you met with General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I read all four upon taking over the assignment, during the period of transfer, so in January 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And it would appear that - and we're looking at the video - that one of these options, in fact, was a topic of conversation with General Mladic, at your first meeting. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke about the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Did you discuss these four options when you spoke with the Dutch authorities prior to meeting with General Mladic, though after speaking with General Nicolai; in other words, between 6.00 and 9.00 you said that you spoke with the Dutch authorities. Did you mention the four options?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were not mentioned. There was no need to, because there was no need to leave, for certain reasons, the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you -- the last option talks about taking the population with you, does it not?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] That's correct. [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Was that option concretely discussed with the Dutch authorities? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer that because I wasn't present at those meetings, and I don't know what the outcome was of those discussions. So the answer is no, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm not asking whether you were part of those discussions. I'm talking about when you had the discussions with them. You told us that you had a conversation with the Dutch authorities. So my question is very simple. When you spoke with the Dutch authorities, did you mention option 4, that is, going -- evacuating with the population?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not discuss options.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you discuss this option with General Nicolai when you spoke to him or he spoke to you, at 1755, earlier?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether I discussed it at that point. After the discussions with Mladic, I also spoke with Brantz. There were so many meetings during that time that I don't remember prior to which meeting or after which meeting I discussed what. Options may have been discussed, but if you're talking to the withdrawal of DutchBat from the enclave, I said that's impossible, given the circumstances at hand concerning the population. So to me personally, departure from the safe area was definitely not an option.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm not talking --

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: So it was not discussed. May I add that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, we know that -- or we've heard, I should say, that the night before - that would be July 10th - you had a meeting with the Muslim authorities in Srebrenica, and I believe it might be the Muslim commanders; correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. With the Muslim commander and with the opstina, the civil authorities of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And at that point, you had told them that there would be 40 or 50 airstrikes the next day, and so there was no need for them to counter-attack because they would be in the zone of death, or words to that effect; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say there would be 40 or 50 airstrikes. I said that there would be sufficient aeroplanes at 6.00 in the morning, and I discussed horizontal, I believe 84, because we're talking about a killing box, or killings, and everything that moved in that zone would be destroyed by aeroplanes. That's what was discussed and what I spoke to the military and civil authorities about at night.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, we know the next day -- well, incidentally, based on that information that you were providing the Muslim commanders, they didn't carry out that counter-offensive towards the Serbs as they had planned; correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Quite honestly, the discussion was fairly unilateral on my behalf. The people I spoke to and never saw after that were really caught between a rock and a hard place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: And when I arrived, I saw a lot of military. I would like to state explicitly here that they probably already had plans that had been activated, plans that made me say afterwards: If I had known, I could have responded. I want to say two things: First, the breakout of the Muslim men; and second, in the case of the collection of the enclave, that I would be facing 50.000 refugees, largely men -- excuse me, women, and elderly people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the next day, we know that the airstrikes did not come in the numbers that you had expected, and in fact came too little, too late, for all intents and purposes; correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, my question is rather simple: Before 1755 hours, before five minutes to 6.00 p.m., did you have any other conversations with General Nicolai? Because it would appear, at least, as early as noon, that the situation had deteriorated to such a degree that Srebrenica was lost, the enclave was lost, for all intents and purposes. Yes, that was the question.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly when and how often, and please don't hold this against me. I don't remember exactly when and how often I spoke with General Nicolai, but there were infinite talks. They could have taken five minutes, we could have had extended discussions about air support or no air support, option, no option, what do I do with the population, what don't I do with the population. And the same happened with Brantz. So at this time, I don't know when or how often I spoke with whom. You can't expect me to have a record nine years later of the times and subjects of my discussions with whom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. What about in that little notebook of yours that you don't want to share with us? Could you look into it and see whether there's something in there that might tickle a memory or two.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I'll be more than happy to have it copied so I wouldn't have to tax you with looking it over.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Tuesday, 11 July. I have quite a few notes from that day, as is indicated in my book. They're primarily about receiving air support or not receiving air support, as I just mentioned. I spoke by telephone with Colonel Brantz on a few occasions and talked with him about that. At 10.00 in the morning, Nicolai called me, or I called Nicolai at 10.00 in the morning, and there was a discussion between Balen and Zagreb on subjects such as UNPROFOR and Srebrenica being shelled. That concerned the blocking positions. It was also about that there would be no aeroplanes arriving. At 10 past 10.00, I spoke with BH command by telephone, so that would be Nicolai or his representative, about the request for close air support. That was ten minutes later. At 10 past 12.00, I received a phone call from BH command, from Sarajevo, that is, about the air support. I was told that it had been improved then. I received several phone calls from sector north-east about air support. At 1.15, I received a call from BH command, and I was asked whether certain essential parts of the section of the battalion had been fired at, and I said yes and that we had wounded too. And they said that an airstrike would come within 15 minutes. Somewhat later, around 4.00 p.m., I reported to Sarajevo, and five or ten minutes later I reported to the north-east command in Tuzla. And that brings me to the conversation with General Nicolai at five to 6.00 on that day. I have no notes, or very few notes, on each individual conversation that I had that day because my phone was ringing off the hook. But I'm sure you'll understand that there were several conversations with sector BiH and Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I take it it was not conveyed to you that on July 10th Janvier had been reluctant to issue such airstrikes or close air support, and he had told this at a meeting to Akashi that morning at approximately 8.30 because he believed that the ABiH, that is, the Muslim army, was the real root of the problem in Srebrenica and that Janvier had expressed his convictions that the Muslim army, the ABiH, was capable of defending the enclave but had clearly chosen not to do so, so that the Bosnian Muslims were putting now pressure on the UN to defend Srebrenica. Was that conveyed to you, sir, about Janvier's reluctance to issue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Could we have a source of this? Is it NIOD or --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I was just going to get to that. NIOD part 3, chapter 6, section 11, page 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer is no. I'm not familiar with the contents of the discussions at the force commander level, that is General Janvier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. It does say that on that particular day you had made a request that is, that Akashi had made a request for close air support when the city came under fire. They say that you wrote this in your book, the one that you have there. And that your request was not granted, based on "incomplete target list." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I requested close air support several times during those six days, and it would exceed the scope to explain the problems to the Court here about the request for close air support. In this context, from the end of May, the upper echelons were very restrictive about granting such support, but I had various conversations with General Nicolai about if the VRS fired directly at the observation posts and if the city was under direct fire and there were casualties and injured, then I thought that was cause, given the objective list that we had submitted in advance. That would be cause for me to receive close air support. This was a very ongoing discussion, and I know what the results were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Very well. If we could get back to this document, because -- and I must apologise to Mr. Usher first for standing there. Finally, we're going to continue. Now, on that same day, July 11th, it says here that Prime Minister Kok found it difficult to choose between doing something and doing nothing. The discussions with Voorhoeve - I think I'm pronouncing it correctly - which Voorhoeve had held with Akashi were raised, and they heard through the American military attache in The Hague that the United States were under the impression that Akashi had even already requested the evacuation of DutchBat." Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Nobody informed you?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It then goes on to say: "It was also known that Janvier in Zagreb and Nicolai in Sarajevo were evaluating the situation." Then if we go down to the very last paragraph on page 1, it says: "Meanwhile, Nicolai had telephoned mad Mladic and passed on the latest details to the Defence Crisis Management Centre. Refugees were being admitted to the compound in Potocari. There were no casualties or wounded among the Dutch. All ops would be abandoned. DutchBat had been forced to leave the compound in Srebrenica and all UN personnel were now centred on the Potocari compound. Nicolai also reported that Karremans intended to negotiate with Mladic on that evacuation. Brantz reported that Tuzla and the VRS had offered an evacuation of the Dutch, representatives of the non-governmental organisations, and also of the population, with the exception of able-bodied men." And there are some footnotes. There's footnote 4 and footnote 5, making reference, and this would appear to have been from daily reports and a statement from Nicolai and a statement by Brantz, and then some notes, I believe, from a -- I can't pronounce their name - it's N-e-i-s-i-n-g-h. In any event, were you aware of that, that at some point in time, at least according to NIOD, that Nicolai had telephoned Mladic?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's -- I'm not familiar with that. There were no discussions about that. This is the first time I'm seeing the contents of this Ministerial Council and the discussions there. The information was not passed on at an early stage, and I believe they were discussing evacuation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I take it -- so it wasn't discussed -- when you spoke with Nicolai at five minutes to 6.00, this wasn't discussed, and I take it at some other point it was never discussed. Later on that day, or some other day, it was never brought to your attention?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I think I answered that before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I just want to be very clear. These are not trick questions, Mr. Karremans. In fact, I'm trying to help you out here. Now, did you ever become aware that while you were there negotiating with Mladic, that Nicolai, who was your superior, was also speaking with Mladic?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Were you aware of anyone else negotiating with Mladic that was higher, at some other level, either military or civil?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Were you privy to discussions that were going above your head, I should say, you know, in other places, that is. Because you were in Srebrenica. Were you ever keeping abreast of --

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Nee."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, page 2 of the same part of the NIOD report, part 3, chapter 7, section 4, states at the second paragraph, last sentence, or last two sentences: "Karremans conferred with Mladic on the admission of aid convoys, unopposed departure of the refugees and of the battalion, along with the weapons, nor was it a coincidence that the attack took place a week before the realisation of the Rapid Reaction Force, and a week before DutchBat was relieved." I don't know what that's about, but it's here. At least the NIOD report indicates that you, upon conferring with Mladic, one of the topics was the unopposed departure of the refugees. Would you accept that portion of the NIOD report, as it's stated here?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you permit me to get back to your first question, for the record?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Rapid Reaction Force.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your question before that. You asked whether I had been informed that there were higher-level discussions about the departure of the battalion. I didn't give you a good answer. I'll answer you again for the record. At five minutes to 6.00, Nicolai discussed the resupply of people battalion and medical support [In English] [Previous translation continues]... of the battalion is in study. [Interpretation] and several other subjects. This means that the withdrawal of the battalion was being studied at a high level and that in due time I would be informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Are you sure you don't want to give us a copy of that? Okay. It would make it easier. All right. Now, if we go on to the third paragraph, in the middle it says -- because I don't want to read everything. It just says: "Karremans was free to act according to his own judgement. This had proved essential in order to prevent loss of life and it also became clear that this had always been given the highest priority in discussions with Karremans." So would it be -- is this correct, that you had sort of -- I won't say carte blanche, but you did have the discretion to use your own judgement, and you were not being micro-managed at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it doesn't say that. I explained to you yesterday that I was the only negotiator, or rather, this morning, although I had requested negotiators at a higher level. This is a fait accompli. I was there to negotiate, after six days of warfare. There was no carte blanche, but there was a foundation for guidelines issued, or to be issued, from Tuzla and/or Sarajevo. It was not a carte blanche for Lieutenant Colonel Karremans to take care of things at his discretion. The conditions were not suitable for that, especially when we're talking about human lives, not even -- you need to consider the wounded and the population. So under the circumstances, you have to have a backup and you have to receive guidelines. And that's what it says here, or at least that's what it's intended to convey.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, going back -- going further down, if I could just get to the -- I'm just going to read about the last -- starting from the last paragraph on page 2. It says -- because this was about the meeting that was ongoing: "The meeting also led to questions about responsibilities and a discussion on evacuation plans. It became clear that the UN was responsible for the negotiations. Evacuation without the consent of the warring factions was only possible with the support of NATO, and the United States would have to take the initiative. It was a risky operation because it would have to be done using helicopters. The time for preparation was three days, and this seemed hardly acceptable under the circumstances, yet inevitable. Only the United States were able to carry out such an operation independently. All other variants would have to be subject to negotiations. The American and French governments had offered to assist with a possible evacuation." It then goes on to say: "The issue of emergency measures to deal with refugees was also raised in the meeting of the Ministerial Council. Only those present did not know the location where provisions had to be made. The most urgent requirement was to find a safe haven. The situation, which had developed, would without doubt lead to ethnic cleansing. Negotiations with the Bosnian Serbs would therefore have to continue for as long as possible, but, on the other hand, there was only sufficient food in Potocari to last for 24 hours." Would you agree with that, that there was only food for 24 hours, first of all, and were you aware of these discussions at this high level?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was not aware of these discussions between the Ministerial Council and the Defence Crisis Management Centre. Obviously, the Minister of Defence spoke with several people, high-ranking officers in the Netherlands. Your second question about food supplies: There was no food. The battalion had no food. And what we had was shared with the population as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And further --

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In other words, there was a need to take action in terms of time, for the population. If there's no food and an epidemic breaks out, then all normal life, such as in a village or city continues - I'm talking about babies being born, people dying - everything has to be taken care of despite the circumstances. So there was an emergency situation, with a capital E. There was an emergency situation. Something had to be done as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. I agree with you. I take it providing bread and water to those refugees would not amount to a war crime. I mean, if it was suggested that members of the Bratunac Brigade were --

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Not at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: What's the relevancy?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Based on what I've got, I'll move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And finally, in this report, it seems, since we've been discussing about the evacuation of the DutchBat, and there's a discussion about the refugees that we've just had, it goes on, on the third paragraph, the last sentence, it says: "A scenario which saw DutchBat leaving, taking along all refugees was difficult to imagine." It says that, and I wanted to be fair, lest there be any insinuation that I was taking it out of context. Now, were you aware of any discussions among the Muslims themselves, you know, either at the local level or in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Well, because I had little contact. I was in touch with Ramiz during the six days once in a while, but we did not discuss evacuation or what would happen afterwards. My final discussion was the one I mentioned this morning. I believe that was on the evening of the 10th or the 11th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: On that particular time, on the 10th, was the discussion of the evacuation of the civilian population discussed?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Because it had not taken place yet. And what I mentioned earlier may have been a plan, and the mission -- although the breakout was already in progress and we didn't know about that at the time either. So the disclosure of information was rather unilateral.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But if I understood your testimony, at least from the 6th to the 10th, there had been a lack of response to your requests for assistance or close air support. Were you that supremely confident on the night of the 10th of July that there would be sufficient air support the next day that this option or eventuality was not necessary to even consider and discuss?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And I take it -- would it be fair to say that had those airstrikes or close air support come in on time, as you had expected, the enclave would have remained?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That is a suggestive question. I can't answer that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I was just asking. I didn't -- wasn't trying to suggest anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, well, Mr. Karnavas. It's time for a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I was just going to say that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You read my mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Witness, do you want to say something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I can't answer this question, because it's the same question as if you had had armament, would then the safe area still have existed? So the answer is: I won't answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We quite understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Witness. We will, we'll take our break and we'll resume at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, before we -- I had asked you whether you were aware of the sentiments expressed by Muslim authorities, and you said that you did not know. Before we get to those documents, I thought I'd conclude with one last document with respect to the UN's position, and this is from part 3, chapter 7, section 6 of the NIOD report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I could have the assistance once again, and I do apologise for ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We see here on the first page, second paragraph, it talks about a meeting with Akashi on 11 July, which started at 1830, so that would have been some 35 minutes after your conversation with General Nicolai. Incidentally, Akashi, you do know who he is, or who he was at the time?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And he was above Janvier? Okay. You're shaking your head. We need to make a record.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yeah, I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, it says here, go to the last paragraph. It says: "The fundamental request question for Janvier remains as to why the ABiH had not deployed the weapons available against VRS. Janvier estimated that 1.500 to 1.800 VRS troops had been involved in the attack, as well as a squadron, four or five tanks. He wondered why the ABiH had not been able to deal with a concentration of VRS troops and what the ABiH had in fact done to assist in the defence of Srebrenica. It was clear to Janvier that the ABiH had shown little zest for battle. Janvier also considered that Mladic would begin to demand that the ABiH lay down its weapons. Zagreb, however, did not have any information as to where the ABiH was in the area around Srebrenica." It then goes on to state: "Akashi then raised the possibility of allowing the refugees from Srebrenica to go to Serbia, in view of the closeness of the border. But he also realised that this would mean crossing the territory of the Republika Srpska and that the population would want to go to Tuzla. The local UNHCR staff in Srebrenica had already made it clear that everybody preferred to leave the enclave. An evacuation was mainly a mass logistical operation, in Akashi's opinion, for which the Bosnian government would have to give its consent." Were you aware of this ongoing conversation that was taking place, this meeting?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I did know that during our meeting, this UNHCR representative was present and mentioned the talks he had conducted with his counterpart, on a higher level, at Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Do you recall whether General -- or Mr. Janvier had informed you of any meetings that he would be attending and that perhaps he would be getting back to you with any other --

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Finally if we could go to the last paragraph of this page, the second-to-last. It says: "The discussions foundered on the urgency of the problem to first get the refugees out of Srebrenica, even though it was possible that similar problems would arise in Zepa and Gorazde during the next few days. But Akashi did not want to brush aside the thoughts of Boutros-Ghali. They had to be considered. Others, however, did push aside his thoughts. A separation of men and women under the eyes of UNPROFOR would be a disgrace of highest orders and would capture the full attention of the media. It was decided to go down two routes: UNHCR would have to establish a plan for the evacuation of the population, and Zagreb would have to inform New York of the problems regarding the enclaves. The estimation during this meeting was that the VRS would not be able to manage 20.000 refugees. The Bosnian Serbs would want to be rid of them. This would be the start of the forced deportation, and UNPROFOR would be accused of helping it along. Akashi was not overly pessimistic. 80 per cent of the population of Srebrenica were already refugees." Were you ever aware of this?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of this discussion, as I said before. But when I look at the analysis, then I would say it makes sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if this meeting did in fact take place, as it would appear on July 11th, at 6.30 p.m., about 35 minutes after your conversations with General Nicolai, and if they're talking about the separation of men, and if we consider earlier, where I showed you where it appeared that General Nicolai had a conversation with Mladic, can we draw a conclusion, or do you allow for the possibility that General Nicolai had been in contact with Mladic even before you showed up?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: He's asking for speculation, and also, we don't know about the separation here, whether it -- on what it was based. That's speculation in itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it is a question of speculation, and the witness, you know, testified that he didn't know anything about this meeting. And of course, you cannot ask any question concerning whether Mladic has been informed about that. As for the second issue, here the separation of men and women is mentioned here. I think, you know, the Defence counsel is entitled to ask a question around here. But there must be sufficient basis, and you could ask -- you could rephrase your question to see whether there was really any separations of men and women in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. I haven't got to Potocari yet, Your Honour, but I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Was -- when you spoke with General Nicolai, did he inform you at any point during that discussion of the potentiality of the separation of the able-bodied men from the women and children?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But it would appear, would it not, from at least if we were to accept the NIOD report, that this was being discussed about 35 minutes after you had your conversation with General Nicolai?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I don't know how this witness can assist. It says here what it says, and the witness said he wasn't aware of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: But under the facts it's very clear that after 35 minutes, you know, this meeting took place. Certain issues were discussed, which the witness did not take part in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I just wanted the record to reflect that, Your Honour, but I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, it also says here, does it not, that it would appear that they were counting on the Bosnian Serbs not being able to manage the evacuation of 20.000-some refugees?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: It's the same point as before. It says what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It becomes relevant at some point, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think that is clearly reflected in that report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You could ask the witness's estimation, the ability of the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I was going to do that at some point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Because, you know, he's an eyewitness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did -- in your conversation with General Janvier, did the discussion ever come up as to whether or how it would be possible to evacuate all those people that were in Potocari at the time, you know, the logistics?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. For I never talked to General Janvier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, what about Nicolai?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: At first, at the time we are -- at the point in time where we are now, I didn't talk to him either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Was the discussion -- was there ever a discussion about whether the Serbs would be able to evacuate the large numbers of refugees that had gathered in Potocari, the logistics of it?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. To the extent that we could not imagine it, that they would be capable of doing it, considering the large number of people that would have to be transported within a relatively short period, considering the humanitarian circumstances the population was in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I take it, speaking of humanitarian circumstances, it was necessary, was it not, during that period of time, if there was an evacuation to occur, that it occur as expeditiously as possible? Would that be fair to state?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: By any way, when you got your orientation prior to coming to Bosnia, or thereafter, did you ever become acquainted with a concept, All People's Defence?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. All, meaning all of us, All People's Defence, a concept that existed and was ingrained in the military doctrine of the JNA, which the BiH, or on both sides, the Serbs and the Muslims, had incorporated as their nascent armies were coming into fruition?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. That's closing argument, I take it. I don't understand why it's relevant at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I'll give Mr. Karnavas some leeway to try this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you. I need some leeway on this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Were you aware of the fact that the -- during the JNA period and thereafter, under the former Yugoslavia, that there was a -- this concept, as part of the military doctrine, along with the civilian protection, where all of the people would be mobilised on a moment's call to assist? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, that's too far, because the witness has already answered the question. Were you aware of that? The witness says no. If the witness doesn't know this concept, there's no follow-up questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I added "civilian protection" on the second one. If I could just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: That's a kind of new concept.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I don't think you can get, you know --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. Very well, Your Honour

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: -- anything from this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But just one last question. I'm not going to ask you about this doctrine, since you are unfamiliar with it. But the speed with which the mobilisation process occurred caused you to jump to some conclusion, did it not?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean the speed at which the refugees were moved away?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, the speed with which the buses were able to show up. Did that not -- I mean, was not some sort of circumstantial evidence that assisted you in formulating some sort of an opinion?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have an opinion, I formed an opinion on that, in the sense that we were highly surprised at the speed with which a great number of coaches and trucks were collected to do that shortly after the morning meeting of July the 12th, and the speed with which they became available. And I said, amongst others, to the battalion staff: How is it possible that one can get together such a large number of vehicles in such -- so short a time? And therefore, I concluded to myself that it was a preplanned operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And it seems that it took the NATO by surprise as well, because, according to the NIOD report on July 13th they were brainstorming on the feasibility of the emergency evacuation. And that could be found part 3, chapter 9, section 1, page 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, that's just an argument. I mean, he's not even asking a question to the witness on this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Were you aware --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I don't think that's necessary. This comment is not necessary. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think we have to go to Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We're just -- we're almost there, Your Honour. We're almost there. And I totally agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, just -- I'd asked you about whether you are aware of the sentiments being expressed or discussed by the Muslims, and you said no. Were you aware that on July 11, that Sacirbey do you know who Sacirbey was by any chance?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Who was he, just for the record?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, at that time, he was minister of foreign affairs, or a representative in the United Nations organisations, at least, or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if I could have the kind assistance of Mr. Usher. And I'm looking at part 3, chapter 9, section 2, again of the NIOD report. And I believe we gave that, for the record, an identification number of 210. It states here -- we're going to go through this rather quickly. It says here, first paragraph, last sentence: "Nicolai advised Voorhoeve" - I hope I'm pronouncing it right - "to instruct DutchBat to give maximum assistance to the displaced persons. Voorhoeve consented and told Nicolai to inform Karremans of his decision. This took place immediately." It then goes on to say that: "During the discussion with Nicolai, which took place 1630 hours, there was, according to Voorhoeve, no longer an emergency situation with regard to DutchBat. The enclave had fallen and the battalion could concentrate on humanitarian tasks before leaving." So this would have appeared that this conversation took place after you spoke with General Nicolai; correct? Between Nicolai and Mr. Voorhoeve? Or was that before?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Then later on it says that, in the middle of the next paragraph, it says that -- actually, I'll read the whole paragraph: "On the afternoon of 11 July, Voorhoeve appeared to have already dropped the idea of getting DutchBat out of the enclave as soon as possible. This can also be deduced from a discussion with Sacirbey, the Bosnian minister of foreign affairs, which took place sometime in the same afternoon. Voorhoeve had assured Sacirbey that the Dutch troops would stay in Srebrenica until all the civilians had been evacuated. Sacirbey then demanded that the entire population, including the soldiers, be protected and evacuated. Voorhoeve agreed." Were you aware of this conversation between -- I guess that was the Minister of Defence of the Netherlands with the Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Bosnian Muslim government in --

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we go to the last part of this page, it says: "Around 10.00 on the evening, at 11 July, Akashi reported to New York that he intended to instruct DutchBat to stay in the enclave until negotiations had been conducted on the departure of the population. Until then a 'substantial presence' was needed in the enclave, and DutchBat had to remain armed. Akashi wanted to offset this against what he thought was still the wish of the Dutch government, namely, to pull out the Dutch troops as soon as possible. Only when a satisfactory agreement had been reached on the departure of the displaced persons would Akashi be prepared to negotiate a withdrawal of DutchBat. By now, the UN staff in Zagreb had also decided that a continued UN presence was important for providing humanitarian aid. The conclusion was that as soon as this necessity no longer existed, there would no longer be a case for a UN presence and DutchBat would leave the enclave." And then it goes on: "But there was a hidden agenda. Akashi had his own reasons for keeping DutchBat in Srebrenica for the time being. He was afraid that a departure might induce the troop-contributing nations to want to withdraw their own units from Zepa and Gorazde." A rather cynical point of view, might I add. Now, were you aware of all of these things?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Was this ever communicated to you?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may -- just one moment. One last moment. I believe we're through with this part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Usher. Now, I have another document -- a couple more documents to go. So now we know at least on the 11th we have the minister of foreign affairs of the Muslims wanting the evacuation of the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now if I can show I part 3, chapter 6, section 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I was waiting for a question. Otherwise it's just a comment. I wasn't sure what the purpose was --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The purpose was to assist, it's a looping process. I'm going down the road to show that there is more than one sentiment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, if it is a statement from the Defence, maybe that's the position held by the Defence counsel, and according to that document. I guess at the end you are going to propose the admission of that document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And the Prosecution has the right to cross-examine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Certainly, absolutely, and we encourage that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, maybe the way of presenting your evidence could be changed, you know, because on the whole transcript, we see you're reading the whole paragraph, and the answer from the witness is: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And what I'm trying to demonstrate, Your Honour - because I need the gentleman's answers - is to show that while he is in Srebrenica trying to deal with the situation there, decisions have been made above him and decisions have been trickled down, and maybe he has gotten one portion, one morsel, I should say, of the information and so that the decision to evacuate everybody was not the brainchild of Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. Can we now argue our case?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I was asked a question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's clearly what's going on. He's using the document to argue his case whether the witness is involved or not. Now, if the witness is involved, that's perfectly -- there's some appropriateness to it, but just to go through the document and then to take out the time that is ticking away to argue his case, I've got to stand up at that point. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. I entirely agree with the objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I take Mr. McCloskey's objection, Your Honour, to heart. But I still have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And put it into action.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I'm trying to improvise, Your Honour. I do have two documents left. If I could show you this document. I'm going to go to page 3. And this is a reference to a gentleman by the name of Osman Suljic, S-u-l-j-i-c.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you know this gentleman, sir? I believe he was the war president.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And he was the war president in Srebrenica; correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I could go to the last paragraph. It says here that Suljic did indeed raise the alarm with the Bosnian authorities in the form of a letter to President Izetbegovic and ABiH Commander Rasim Delic. In this letter, Suljic sketched the situation at 1900 hours on 9 July. "The command structure in the enclave had begun to collapse and the 28th Division was no longer capable of stopping the VRS from entering the city. Chaos and panic prevailed and the civilian authorities were faced with the problem of saving the population. Suljic proposed a meeting between the Bosnian political and military leaders and those of the Republika Srpska to establish whether it would be possible to open a corridor to allow the population to travel to the territory of the Muslim-Croat Federation under international supervision. Suljic insisted on an answer within 24 hours. Izetbegovic did not react." Did you, by any chance, Mr. Karremans, have any conversations with the war president to discuss this matter?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did he at any point in time - because it seems this is 7.00 in the evening, 7.00 in the evening on July 9th - did he by any chance come to you to inform you of his concerns and as to whether any measures should be taken to evacuate the population from Srebrenica, as he had been requesting from President Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not as far as I remember. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just lastly on this issue: Were you aware that there had been a plan, that a plan did exist, both for the defence and the evacuation of the enclave, a plan that predated the incident surrounding Srebrenica, from 6 to 11 July? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to a plan of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. A plan of the -- yes.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Would it surprise you that you would find that such a plan existed in the NIOD report, chapter 6, section -- part 3, chapter 6, section 24? Would that surprise you?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That surprises me, because during the many talks that have been going on with the leadership of the ABiH and all the talks were fed back, in all of that, I don't remember ever talking -- discussing a defence plan, withdrawal, or anything of the sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: However, I agree with the analysis which Suljic gave on the 9th concerning the collapse of the defence, because we had noticed that ourselves, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I think we're ready for Potocari. And I want to thank you for assisting me to go through all of these documents, and I appreciate the indulgence of the Trial Chamber on this one, as well as the Prosecutor's indulgence. Now, I don't want to talk about the second and third meeting, because we don't have enough time. If I had four or five days, we would go into this in more detail. But in light of the limited time that we do have, let's talk about the 12th and the 13th -- yeah, the 12th and the 13th, starting with after your third meeting with General Mladic, which would have been on the morning of the 12th. Could you please tell us: After you left that meeting, where did you go? After you left Fontana.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I returned directly to the compound in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, could you please tell us: During those days - because there seems to be some dilemma - were you in charge or were you incapacitated, sick in some way, and Major Franken had taken over as acting commander?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You were still in charge, still in command?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Even if you're sick for a night, then you're still in charge. You're always in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But were you sick on that day, the 12th and the 13th?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked me the same question the day before yesterday, and I started thinking about whether that was the case. I was sick once. I explained to you that half the battalion was sick, as far as the food supply was concerned. And I remember that evening, but I would really need to go very far back in my memory. But about that evening, no. The evening from the 12th to the 13th, so much happened and so much had to be arranged that I cannot remember having been sick for any reason at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And just -- the conversation we had was when we shared that beer, that little time that we were able to have together upon your arrival; right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I'm referring to. And I also explained to you that it happened a week later and had nothing to do with the situation at the time. And if you're referring to -- if you're referring to a division of responsibility, it's very difficult under these circumstances, because so much had to be done and I had given Major Franken carte blanche to carry things out, and I knew in advance or discussed it after the fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, okay. Well, you're anticipating some very large areas of discussion, but I just want to make sure I nail this one down. On the 12th and the 13th, your health was fine. You didn't have diarrhoea, as some have claimed was the case?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, we're going to talk about the division of labour or, in military parlance, I guess it would be the division of functions, between commander and assistant commander, or Chief of Staff. But first of all, could you please tell us what you, as the commander, what functions did you retain that you were going to be involved in on a hand-to-hand --

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] All of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Except, and you should consider this in the available time frame of 24 hours a day, minus a few hours for other matters that I needed to delegate a few things, and that's a very normal part of the organisation. But I remained responsible for whatever I delegated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I take it there might be some notes in that little notebook of yours that you've yet to let us take a peek at, about the days. There may be some little notes in that little notebook.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They're also in this book.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. All right. Very well. Now, let's start with what duties you delegated. Could you please tell us what duties you delegated to Major Franken.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. It's easy. In a battalion staff, there's a commander, a deputy commander, a staff officer, an intelligence officer, an operations officer, and a logistics officer, plus many other officers and sub-officers. From 6 through 11 July, my deputy was in Tuzla. My operations officer, a major, was in the Netherlands, waiting to return to the enclave. In the end, 80 troops were unable to return because they -- because of the closure of the enclave. So under the tension of 6, 11, 12, and 13, we had to distribute the tasks. The additional tasks I issued to Major Franken was to run the operations and provide military supervision to the companies and units that constituted the battalion. This is never outside the knowledge of the commander, and if I, as a commander, say that's not happening, then it doesn't happen. He was already responsible for logistics operations within the battalion. So he was assigned an additional task that, considering his experience in previous functions, he was quite able to perform this task. Staff and intelligence were not a problem, because I did have officers for that. So I was missing two extremely important officers in a situation such as this one, the deputy commander and the operations officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. We may need to ask you to slow down a little bit so as not to overtax --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter was no sound.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We may need you to slow down a little bit so as not to overtax the interpreter. Okay. Well, in light of these tasks that you had delegated to Major Franken, may I ask you: Who was in charge of liaisoning or dealing with the Serb counterparts, you know, at the highest level?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is the highest level Sarajevo and somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please be specific. I'm responsible for everything, and I was also responsible for external communications, both in the military hierarchy and toward the ABiH and to the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, who was dealing directly with your Serb counterparts, you know, the commanders? There was Mladic, there was Zivanovic, or Krstic. Who was dealing with them?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was. But there was never any opportunity in the preceding period, except for occasionally a conversation with Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we know that you met with General Mladic on three occasions. Once you got to Potocari, could you tell us who was in charge on the Serbian side, the VRS side, of that entire operation, if you know.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, was Mladic there the entire time, the 12th and the 13th?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I wasn't with him 24 hours a day. But I did meet him on a few occasions, on the 12th and 13th, and I referred to that in my book, based on my notes. After that, he was gone for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. When Mladic was not around on the 12th and the 13th, as we all know in this courtroom, because he was only there off and on, with whom were you dealing? Who was his acting commander or the person in charge?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. At best, I can refer to a contact, somebody who would get in touch with us, or we could get in touch with them via the interpreter. As I mentioned, when problems arose concerning aid and so on, the name was Jankovic, and we interacted with him if he came to us -- yeah, he basically came to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But I guess -- because the military, as I understand it, is a rather formal and rigid institution. When the commander isn't there, normally there is an acting commander or deputy commander or somebody who's left in charge. So did Mladic inform you as to who was in charge that you would need to deal with specifically?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The witness was asked the question before and he said: I don't know. Just the last question. The question -- the last answer. The question was from Mr. Karnavas: When Mladic was not around and so on. And then there was sort of a compound question. First: Who are you dealing with, and second, who was his acting commander. And then the witness answered: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. It's all in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So when Mladic wasn't there, you didn't know who you were supposed to interact with?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Again, because Mr. Karnavas puts two questions, two points into one question. And the witness answers to one. Who was in charge, and who are you dealing with? And it's very difficult, and perhaps unfair, than just to take out one basically answer of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think those questions have been answered by this witness already. He mentioned a name Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. I'll go around --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Was Jankovic the acting commander, sir?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know who the deputy was, who was in charge when Mladic was not present. You referred to a deputy. I don't know. But Jankovic and a person named Nikolic were the battalion's contacts for all interactions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, did you bother to ask, you as the commander, who would be in charge of this operation, since it would appear that you were now responsible for the safety of all those refugees that were there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Again the question is argumentative. He can ask: Did you ask who was in charge? And then just mere reference to bothering and -- I think it's unnecessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, it's not quite, because he's the commander. I can understand if it was some lieutenant, but this is the commander. So I would assume that a commander would ask the other commander: Who am I to deal with? Specifically who is in charge? Somebody has got to be in charge. We can't have all these people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, logically, this question is not very good, because, first, the witness answered he didn't know. If he asked, he will know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Can I ask, Your Honour, why he doesn't know, why he didn't bother to ask the question? Would that be okay? Because as a commander, I would assume -- or were several people in charge?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: It seems to me that you put the blame on this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, I don't, Your Honour. No. This is an issue with command responsibility. That's the whole case. That's why the Prosecution is objecting so much. Because it hurts them to know that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, well, well, well. That's too far. You may put your question to this witness in the simplest way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Who was in charge of the logistics on the Serbian side?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Who was in charge --

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd like to get back to this discussion, if I'm allowed. Under ordinary conditions, a person will introduce his deputy and his most important staff officers. This would happen at the second or third or fourth meeting, so I would know who I would be dealing with or who I could deal with, and then I would have known names. I would have remembered faces, and I could tell somebody: You're the commander, so you should know who you're dealing with. That didn't happen. I gave you two names, because those were the men who regularly came to the CP battalion in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Are you -- were you under the impression that Nikolic was in charge, or was he just a contact person?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, while you were there during the 12th and 13th, and incidentally, I want to make sure that we're clear. Nobody's blaming you for anything or putting you on trial. But while you were there on the 12th and 13th, what exactly were you doing? As concretely as possible.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not possible to be specific, because so much happened on the 12th and 13th, and so much had to be communicated to the outside, and there was so much supervision, with some parts being delegated, that at this point I can't state everything I did. Much of my time was taken up with meetings, with phone calls to higher echelons and national authorities and running all kinds of meetings, supervising and streamlining operations within the battalion. I also needed to supervise the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had to consult with the teams about the wounded. I had to visit the bandaging unit. It was too much to stipulate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you walk around at all?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw more than you want to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. I take it you walked all over the place to make sure everything was going as planned.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Several times I left the compound. Of course, I also walked around inside the compound a few times. I was in the hall with refugees. I visited the areas with all the wounded several times. And in between, I spoke with a lot of people and my own soldiers, as well as the battalion supervisors, my staff, the surgeons, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And it was based on those observations during those -- that period of time that you walked around and spoke to various people that you were able, on the 23rd of July, 1995, to stay -- to put in your statement: I did not witness any individual human rights violation"; right? That was your statement?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was my statement, and I did not observe that personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. I'm not -- I'm just saying personally.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] No. You asked personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, it's right here. If I could -- if we could get this put on the ELMO, perhaps this would assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, before we put that document on the ELMO, I found that it's classified as confidential.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think you have to make sure that -- the reason why, and if there's no absolute necessity, I believe that everybody has got this document. So we better not put it on the ELMO. Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. We have inquired with the provider of that information. It was protected and the protected is lifted, so it can be discussed publicly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. So we could put it on the ELMO. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And we could refer to this as, for identification purposes, as D206. It states here, if we see on the top, it has your name. It would appear that this was taken in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Correct? Is that where this statement was taken, sir?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think the statement was taken in Zagreb, on 23 July. I did several interviews there. One was with an international organisation, human rights -- the human rights organisation, or something like that. And they asked me to make a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And we see in the very first sentence: "I did not witness any individual human rights violations." You stand by that; correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And just to make sure I understood you correctly: During that 12th and 13th of July, you were not confined in your office, but rather, you walked around and engaged in conversations with others? That's a question.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, in your statement here, you do talk about Jankovic being present during the negotiations with Mladic. And then I notice that when you gave your statement to the OTP, the Office of the Prosecution, on 28 September, there you indicated, again, that - and I'm referring to -- it doesn't have a page number, but it's -- the ERN number is 00443296. It states: "Colonel Jankovic, also coordinator of the Srebrenica case, and another colonel whose name I do not recall and who was in charge of logistics."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The version I have, I take it it's the same, because it's the same ERN number, says: "Colonel Jankovic (assistant and possibly also coordinator of the Srebrenica case)."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: "And another colonel whose name I do not recall." Now, of the -- do you know, by any chance, in your little book whether you put the name of the other colonel in there?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] We discussed this before, and I don't know any name for this person. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Can I ask: How is it the commander did not know the name of the person who was in charge of the logistics of this rather massive operation?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't answer that. It's possible. You may not have a very clear impression, although I understand that you've been working on this for three years. You may not clearly understand the circumstances under which a commander operates in that situation and what such a commander is doing. And of course, things escape such a commander that you hear later on. You can't keep abreast of everything. And sometimes you might not remember a name or you might think I'm not dealing personally with this person because Major Franken is -- if I'm referring to logistics, I hope you won't hold it against me that I don't know this man's name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No. And we've been trying to convey all of that, by the way.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] I understand. I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, this person, this colonel who was in charge of the logistics, do you know - concretely, if you could tell us - how exactly he was handling the logistics, what exactly was he doing?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Can you help us out here, and maybe, since we have two colonels, Jankovic and this other person, do you know which of the two was above -- you know, who was number one, who was number two, or were they both at the same level?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] I don't know. [Interpretation] I don't know. I don't know whether they were at the same level. They were contacts only. But Nikolic was at a much lower level, but I'm sure you understood that. During the course of the investigation, Jankovic and this other colonel were counterparts. And the other without a name was primarily responsible for logistics. You asked me how he organised logistics and how he was responsible. I don't know how he organised that. I have no idea. So the answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Nikolic and this particular gentleman had been, or was, the liaison officer between the Bratunac Brigade and UNPROFOR, DutchBat; right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And so you had prior contacts with him, and in fact you write rather extensively and perhaps, you know, rather negatively, about Mr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS [Resumed]
